t: Topic and aim of the lesson
n: In this lecture we will consider the method of immunohistochemistry. Immunohistochemistry, IHC for short, looks for tissue and cell antigens: amino acids, proteins, infectious agents and particular cell populations. Special antibodies are used for this. In differential diagnosis, where routine analysis with haematoxylin and eosin cannot give an answer, IHC serves as a supplementary method. An example from forensic medicine: in death from traumatic brain injury, the protein FOXO3a was positive in all 15 cases and negative in 15 controls. The plan of the lesson is as follows: the history of the method, its applications, limitations, interpretation of the result and quantitative assessment, then analysis of a forensic medical study.

t: What is IHC? A "conversation" with cells
n: IHC is the general name for methods that identify tissue components, that is antigens, with specific antibodies. The antibody becomes visible through staining. Note: in cell preparations this method is called immunocytochemistry, while some authors apply this term to tissue sections as well. In Brandtzaeg's view, staining cell markers is a "conversation" with the cells. With the right antibodies, the origin of the cell and its function in the living organism are determined. For this reason Brandtzaeg considers it inappropriate to call IHC merely a descriptive method.

t: The two stages of IHC technique
n: The IHC technique consists of two stages. The first stage is preparation of the specimen, that is fixation and tissue processing, together with the steps of the reaction. In the reaction the order is as follows: first antigen retrieval, then blocking of non-specific sites and endogenous peroxidase, then the primary antibody. The second stage is interpretation of the expression obtained and its quantitative assessment. The diagram shows the sequence: fixation and tissue processing, antigen retrieval and blocking, primary antibody and detection, visualisation and counterstaining, and finally interpretation and quantitative assessment.

t: History: from Marrack and Coons to Nakane
n: Now the history of the method. Marrack created reagents against the organisms of typhoid and cholera; a red dye was attached to them. Then in the early 1940s Coons demonstrated antigen in tissue with a fluorescein-labelled antibody against pneumococcus. Nakane used an enzyme-labelled antibody, and in the 1960s it became possible to see the reaction in an ordinary optical microscope. Remember: Coons's method is seen in a fluorescence microscope, and Nakane's enzyme method in an ordinary optical microscope.

t: PAP, APAAP, DAB and colloidal gold
n: At the next stage new methods appeared. PAP, that is peroxidase–antiperoxidase, and APAAP, that is alkaline phosphatase, are unlabelled antibody methods. DAB, that is diaminobenzidine, is the most widely used chromogen for peroxidase and gives an electron-dense precipitate. Colloidal gold particles later led to the method of intracellular, that is subcellular, immunostaining. In the diagram, PAP is linked to the name of Sternberger, APAAP to that of Mason, and DAB to its use in electron microscopy in place of ferritin.

t: Antigen retrieval and the ABC/LSAB systems
n: The method of antigen retrieval was discovered by Huang: epitopes are exposed, and antibody binding is made easier. Hsu proposed the ABC systems, that is avidin–biotin–peroxidase, and LSAB, that is streptavidin–biotin, with a secondary antibody. Once the method was proven on formalin-fixed paraffin tissue, it entered daily diagnosis. This period is called the "brown revolution". That is, the path to daily diagnosis went through these stages: antigen retrieval, the ABC and LSAB systems, and proof on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded material.

Now a case analysis on the history section. Situation: in the early 1940s Coons stained antibodies to pneumococcus with fluorescein and saw the antigen in ultraviolet light, that is in a fluorescence microscope. In the 1960s Nakane labelled antibodies with an enzyme, and the reaction could then be seen in an ordinary light microscope. As a result, the method left the laboratories with fluorescence microscopes and spread among many researchers and pathologists. Question: which discovery was decisive? Into daily practice, the possibility of demonstrating antigen in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue was introduced by antigen retrieval.

About the fields of application of IHC. Immunohistochemistry is used as a supplementary method to determine the genesis and subtype of a tumour. For example, subtyping in lymphoma is carried out in this way. The method is also used to look for the primary focus, that is the source in a metastasis, and to determine prognostic factors and indications for treatment. In addition, benign and malignant growth can be distinguished. Structures, organisms and substances released by cells are also identified.

t: The Werner study: benefit of IHC
n: In the Werner study 3760 specimens were assessed; in 64% of cases IHC was used for diagnostic purposes. According to the chart, 19% was recorded for prognostic factors and indices, and 17% for micro-organisms and structures. Of 835 diagnostic cases, in 83% IHC contributed to a precise diagnosis, and uncertain diagnoses were reduced by 12%. Useful cases totalled 95%. In the remaining 5% the method did not help: the specimen was small, necrosis was extensive or the tumour was too poorly differentiated.

Case analysis on the applications section. Situation: the tumour in the biopsy is morphologically undifferentiated, and haematoxylin and eosin staining gives no answer about its type. Immunohistochemistry determines the histogenesis, type and primary focus of the tumour, reveals prognostic factors and distinguishes benign from malignant growth. In Werner's analysis, in 5% of cases IHC did not help: the specimen was too small, necrosis was extensive or the tumour was excessively poorly differentiated. Question: for what purpose is IHC used in this situation, and in which cases may it give no result?

The first quick question. First question: what is IHC, and what is it called when applied to cell smears? Second question: with what labelled antibody did Coons demonstrate antigen in the early 1940s, and what did Nakane's innovation change? Third question: why is diaminobenzidine, that is DAB, important, and what did it replace in electron microscopy? Fourth question: in Werner's analysis, in what proportion of the 3760 specimens was IHC used for diagnostic purposes, and in how many cases did it contribute to a precise diagnosis? Think about the answers.

About the sequence of reaction steps. After the specimen is prepared, that is after fixation and tissue processing, the reaction steps follow in a set order. After the reaction comes the second stage: interpretation of the expression obtained and its quantitative assessment. Remember: the order of reagents must be strict. A working scheme protects against false results.

The question of fixation. Formalin fixation reversibly reduces immunoreactivity: some antibody binding sites are blocked or damaged. Epitopes are exposed by retrieval methods, but the detection system must nevertheless be sensitive enough to give a strong signal. In Alves's study, on an ovarian tumour, ethanol fixation showed cytokeratin and vimentin better. In formalin, cytokeratin stained better after trypsin, whereas trypsin harmed vimentin; delay in fixation is also dangerous. In ethanol, reactivity was higher and remained good when stored for up to 60 days.

Section thickness and paraffin temperature. The thickness of a section cut from the block should preferably be from 3 to 7 micrometres, that is μm. A section thinner than 3 μm stains very weakly; a section thicker than 7 μm may detach from the slide or make assessment difficult. The section is placed on a slide previously coated with an adhesive, silane or polylysine. Attention: risk of error! Embedding in paraffin at a temperature usually above 60 °C can damage antigenicity.

Amount and selection of specimen. Precise diagnosis is demanded from small specimens, so the amount of specimen is discussed. In most cases one block is sufficient, especially if it contains the border of the tumour and the surrounding parenchyma. The block is taken away from areas of haemorrhage or extensive necrosis; representative tissue away from the tumour is also useful. If possible, tissue previously examined in the frozen state should be avoided.

Antigen retrieval and detection systems. Antigen retrieval, that is HIER, is heat-induced exposure of the epitope, performed in a microwave oven or with moist steam under pressure. ABC, that is the avidin–biotin–peroxidase complex, and LSAB, that is streptavidin–biotin, are the main amplification systems. In the chain of development, EPOS, that is one-step polymer, and CARD, that is catalysed deposition, follow. But there is a paradox: the systems gave new positive results, but non-specificity increased. Swanson rejected a universal method.

Primary antibodies are polyclonal or monoclonal; their capabilities differ. A polyclonal antibody is obtained by immunising an animal, for example a rabbit or goat, binds to many epitopes of one antigen and has high sensitivity. A monoclonal antibody is created from hybridomas, binds to only one epitope and has high specificity. In both cases, a new batch or clone is titrated; the dilution with the greatest contrast between true positive signal and background is chosen. Attention: many epitopes does not mean high specificity. Polyclonal is sensitive, monoclonal is specific.

Choosing the antibody panel is one of the most important aspects of immunohistochemistry, and determines the correct application of the method. According to Jensen and colleagues, the choice of panel and the interpretation of the reaction pattern in each case have the greatest influence on the final diagnosis. The sensitivity of the chosen panel increases with the experience of the pathologist requesting the method and with analysis of clinical data. Prescott and colleagues attributed 42.1 per cent of diagnostic discrepancies in immunohistochemistry to poor antibody selection.

Types of control. An external control is a special tissue section for each antibody. It is included in each panel and confirms the results. The external control is fixed in the same way as the test specimens and goes through the same steps of the reaction. An internal control consists of structures in the specimen under study itself. Attention: it is not a separate section. The internal positive control includes vessels and ducts beside the tumour, in which a positive reaction is expected. The internal negative control includes erythrocytes in a vessel; they are a negative background that has undergone the same processing.

t: Sources of error: reaction and interpretation
n: About sources of error. Bias is an error that skews the result. Although the method is simple, results are interpreted with caution. The result depends directly on the experience of the hand that performed the reaction and the eye that interpreted it. According to the table, reaction bias includes specimen preparation, that is fixation and tissue processing, and the reaction itself, that is antigen retrieval and the detection system. Interpretation bias includes selection, that is choice of antibody panel and clone, and evaluation, that is interpretation of the result and the literature. Remember: reaction bias differs from interpretation bias. The first is technical, the second an error of selection and evaluation.

Quality control programmes. The immunohistochemistry quality control committee of the French Society of Pathology published a report in 1997. According to the report, the two main causes of diagnostic error are failure to use antigen retrieval methods and use of weak amplification methods. There are other international programmes too: the Immunoquery electronic database and UK NEQAS, that is the British external quality assessment scheme, for immunocytochemistry. Controlling the order of reagents with working schemes protects against false results. It is also recommended to record each step and the pattern of each antibody.

Case analysis on technical errors. Situation: in a breast cancer specimen that had been in fixation for a long time or stored for 12 weeks, p53 and Bcl-2 stained weakly. Cause: if a fresh specimen is placed in prolonged fixation, antigenicity falls markedly. Storage on the slide at room temperature for 12 weeks also loses antigenicity. Formaldehyde masks or destroys epitopes. Delay in fixation may also cause loss of immunoreactivity for some antibodies. Question: what is done to prevent this? Control fixation and transport, restore the antigen, and keep the paraffin temperature no higher than 60 °C.

The second quick question. First question: within what range is the thickness of a block section chosen for IHC, and what happens if it is thinner than 3 μm or thicker than 7 μm? Second question: what happens to antibody binding sites in fixation with formaldehyde, and how is it corrected? Third question: how do polyclonal and monoclonal primary antibodies differ, which is more sensitive and which more specific? Fourth question: give examples of external and internal controls. Which structure can serve as an internal negative control?

t: Interpreting the result: quality and subjectivity
n: Interpretation of the result is usually performed qualitatively and subjectively, and quantitative assessment is often regarded as of little importance. The decision often rests on the presence or absence of the molecule. A growing reason for contradictory results in the literature is that what a "positive" result is has not been clearly defined. For example, for S-100 some authors require staining of nucleus and cytoplasm, while others regard cytoplasm alone as sufficient. Attention: in HER2, only staining of the cell membrane is linked to gene amplification. Purely cytoplasmic staining is not equal to membranous staining.

t: A "positive" result: the S-100 and HER2 example
n: The concept of a "positive" result. In many studies, "positive" means brown staining, that is the peroxidase reaction, in any part of the tissue. Look at the table. For S-100, if nucleus and cytoplasm are stained, some authors call it positive. If only cytoplasm is stained, others also regard it as positive. In HER2, staining of cytoplasm alone was regarded as positive in some works, whereas staining of the cell membrane is linked to gene amplification. Attention: in HER2 cytoplasm is not equal to membrane; only membrane staining is linked to gene amplification.

t: The localisation rule and confirming the result
n: The localisation rule. If the localisation of the antigen is known, the pattern of immunoreactivity should correspond to its microanatomical or intracellular distribution. Molecules in cytoplasmic vesicles, that is chromogranin, von Willebrand factor and HMB-45, give granular intracytoplasmic staining. If staining is not as expected, most call it false positive; however, the molecule may also have a function not yet described. In a doubtful case, the result is confirmed with antibodies to other epitopes of the same molecule or with related markers, synaptophysin and chromogranin.

Case analysis on the interpretation section. Situation: a specimen with an antibody to HER2 stained brown, but the staining is only in the cytoplasm, not in the membrane. Question: can this result be called positive, and why is clinical-morphological context needed? Guide: there is staining, but only membranous staining is linked to gene amplification. Expression in different compartments may signify different functions. Conclusion: record brown staining as positive, then interpret it in the context of the molecule's function and the clinical-morphological picture.

t: IHC and ELISA: the common principle
n: IHC and ELISA share a common principle. IHC, that is immunohistochemistry, is an immunological test performed in situ on a tissue section. ELISA, that is enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, has reagents that also work in IHC on a paraffin section. Compare: in ELISA the specimen is serum, in IHC a section from a paraffin block. The reagents are the same. ELISA is accepted as quantitative and widely recognised, while IHC is often regarded simply as "staining". Nevertheless, the quantitative assessment of IHC is statistically linked to Western blot and enzyme immunoassay methods.

Semi-quantitative analysis. Intensity grades, that is zero, weak, moderate and strong, depend on experience and are subjective, so they are undesirable. Distribution is the percentage of stained cells; counting may also be done "by eye". Ki67, p53 and p21 are cell-cycle indices, and the reproducibility of their counts is low. Scoring systems were introduced to reduce differences and are used in selecting patients for treatment, but they are laborious and tiring.

Computer analysis and prospects. Computer-assisted image analysis has been used since the 1980s and for many markers gives a more accurate result than the semi-quantitative method. Under controlled conditions the system surpassed the manual method of many observers and solves the problem of reproducibility of scoring systems. About the future: a one-step reaction, EPOS, reduces incubation steps; semi-automated instruments and microarray technology have also been developed. For the benefit of the patient it is important that the pathologist and clinician speak the same language, combining their knowledge.

The third quick question. First question: what does a "positive" result in IHC usually mean? Answer: the presence of brown, that is peroxidase, staining in any part of the tissue. Second question: which staining in HER2 is linked to gene amplification? Answer: only staining of the cell membrane. Attention: cytoplasm is not equal to membrane. Third question: which assay does IHC resemble? Answer: ELISA, that is enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay: the reagents and the immunological principle are the same. Fourth question: what is superior to semi-quantitative scores? Answer: computer-assisted image analysis; under controlled conditions it is better even than manual analysis by many observers.

t: FOXO3a: the family and its role in the brain
n: Now we turn to the forensic study: FOXO3a. FOXO transcription factors control proliferation, differentiation, metabolism, oxidative stress and cell lifespan. FOXO3a is widely expressed in the brain, especially in the hippocampus, cortex and cerebellum. In mature neurons, FOXOs regulate ROS pathways, neuroinflammation, apoptosis and autophagy. FOXO3a is neuroprotective against ischaemic injury; in traumatic brain injury, that is TBI, its level rises and is linked to the severity of injury.

t: Forensic medicine: the nature of TBI and FOXO3a
n: The nature of TBI and FOXO3a from the forensic medical point of view. Traumatic brain injury, TBI, is disturbance of brain function or signs of brain pathology under the action of an external force on the head. Primary damage occurs immediately, secondary damage over days and weeks: ischaemia, oxidative stress, apoptosis. FOXO3a is a transcription factor regulating apoptosis, neuroinflammation and the response to oxidative stress. The chain is as follows: external force, primary damage, secondary damage, activation of FOXO3a, then apoptosis and inflammation.

Primary and secondary TBI. Primary injury arises immediately from the action of an external force: direct blow, acceleration and deceleration, penetrating injury, blast wave. Secondary injury develops over days and weeks as a result of the cellular inflammatory response following the primary injury: ischaemia, oxidative stress, apoptosis. This division is for teaching purposes only: the two often occur together, but it helps in defining treatment protocols. In primary injury, for example a haematoma, treatment is often surgical, whereas in secondary injury the aim is early identification and prevention of the pathways of cell damage.

Study groups. Fifteen cases of death from TBI were selected: 4 women, 11 men, mean age 43.1. In 8, death occurred immediately, in 7 within 6 hours. Inclusion criteria: cause of death TBI, injury within the previous 24 hours, no history of chronic disease. Control group: 15 non-traumatic brain deaths, 8 women and 7 men, age 49.3. Of these, 5 were aneurysm rupture and 10 acute circulatory arrest. Decomposed or decomposing bodies were excluded from both groups; autopsy was performed within 36 hours after death.

t: Design of the FOXO3a study and the IHC protocol
n: Design of the FOXO3a study and the IHC protocol. The study includes 15 TBI deaths and 15 non-traumatic brain deaths; decomposed bodies were excluded from both groups. Inclusion criterion: cause of death TBI, injury within the previous 24 hours, no history of chronic disease. Protocol steps: fixation in 10% formalin and paraffin embedding, then a 4 μm section. Antigen retrieval was performed in EDTA buffer, in pressurised steam at 100 °C for 90 minutes; polyclonal anti-FOXO3a was used. As a control, the test was performed on breast cancer tissue. Assessment was by two observers on a scale of 0–4.

t: FOXO3a results and the scoring scale
n: FOXO3a results. In all 15 cases of death from traumatic brain injury FOXO3a was positive, and in the 15 controls it was negative. The reaction was assessed with scores from 0 to +4. The scale is as follows: score 0 no staining, score 1 about 25 per cent staining, score 2 about 50 per cent, score 3 about 75 per cent, and score 4 100 per cent staining. Two researchers examined the slides, and if they disagreed a third decided. As survival time after injury lengthened, the FOXO3a reaction strengthened, with a maximum at 6 hours.

Quantitative assessment and statistics. On each IHC section, 20 observations were made in different fields at 100-fold magnification; 3D reconstruction was also done with a confocal microscope. Staining intensity was assessed in a blinded manner by two researchers on a scale from 0 to +4; in case of disagreement a third observer decided. The score was based on the strongest positivity observed; in TBI cases the mean intensity was 2.53, p < 0.05. For ordinal data the Kruskal–Wallis test was used and, if there was a difference, Dunn's post hoc test; the significance level was 5%.

t: Case analysis: FOXO3a and post-mortem diagnosis
n: Case analysis on FOXO3a and post-mortem diagnosis. Situation: in the brain of a person who died several hours after injury, FOXO3a was positive in neurons near the injury. This shows the involvement of FOXO3a in secondary injury after TBI, in the regulation of neuronal apoptosis and autophagy. It may become a promising tool in post-mortem diagnosis. Limitation: the cases are few, 15 TBI and 15 controls, and the study is preliminary. The authors plan to increase the number of cases. Attention: risk of error. In the study the maximum survival time was 6 hours; no conclusions about a longer period can be drawn from these data.

Conclusion. IHC consists of two stages: preparation of the specimen and carrying out the reaction, followed by interpretation of expression and quantitative assessment. Fixation, antigen retrieval, positive and negative controls, and correct choice of the antibody panel determine the reliability of the result. Interpretation requires caution; scoring systems may be subjective, whereas computer analysis gives a more accurate quantitative result. In forensic medicine, FOXO3a has been proposed as a promising tool for post-mortem detection of TBI, but further studies are needed.
